Society · Democracy

Should the state make you vote?

For most Brazilians, voting isn’t a choice: it’s the law. Most democracies let people decide. Who has it right?

By EIC Magazine · 6 min read · Hover over the dotted words to see them in Portuguese

Listen to the article0:00 / 3:28
Speed

On Sunday 4 October, 158.7 million Brazilians are able to vote for president, governors and Congress. For most of them, turning up is not optional. Brazil is one of only 21 countries in the world with compulsory voting, and one of about ten that actually enforce it.

What the law asks

If you are between 18 and 70, the law requires you to vote. If you are 16 or 17, over 70, or cannot read, it lets you choose. The fine for staying at home is tiny: up to R$ 3.51 for each round you miss.

The real cost comes later. Until you justify your absence or pay the fine, the state won’t let you get a passport, sign up for a public-sector exam or enrol at a public university.

And yet millions stay home anyway. In the first round of 2022, 20.95% of voters didn’t show up: more than 32 million people. Some forgot, some were travelling, and some simply refused to let the government tell them what to do.

A rare rule

Most democracies let citizens decide for themselves. Where voting is compulsory, the history is long. Belgium introduced the rule in 1893, and Australia in 1924. Today Australia sends non-voters a fine of AU$20, and turnout rarely falls below 90%.

Belgium is moving the other way. The country stopped punishing non-voters in 2003, and in 2024 the Flemish region no longer made people vote in local elections.

The Chilean experiment

Chile offers the clearest test. In 2012 it let citizens choose, and turnout collapsed: in 2021, only 43% of registered voters took part. Worried that a small, angry minority was deciding for everyone, the country made voting compulsory again in 2022. In the constitutional referendum that September, turnout jumped to 85.8%. Venezuela went the opposite way in 1993, and turnout fell from 82% to 61%.

Duty or freedom?

Supporters say the rule forces politicians to listen to everyone, not only to the most motivated voters. When everybody votes, a party can’t win just by getting its angriest fans to the polls. They also argue that it protects poorer citizens, who are usually the first to stay home when voting is optional.

Critics see it differently. Freedom, they say, includes the freedom not to take part. They warn that forcing uninterested people to vote produces random votes, or votes for sale. Some suggest that Brazil keep the duty to register but let each voter decide whether to turn up.

On Sunday, most Brazilians will vote because they have to. The real question is whether they would go if nobody made them.

“When Chile let people choose, turnout fell to 43%.”Chile, 2021 · voluntary voting

The state should make people vote
